title: What is the `char` type (16-bit unsigned UTF-16 code unit, range 0–65535), why can a `char` hold only a BMP character (supplementary characters like emoji require a surrogate pair — two `char`s), and how do `Character.isHighSurrogate`, `Character.toCodePoint`, and `String.codePointAt` handle characters outside the BMP?
shortTitle: What is the char type, why can it hold only a BMP character, and how do surrogate pairs and code points handle emoji?

s1_definition.profdef: A Java `char` is a 16-bit unsigned integer type holding one UTF-16 code unit in the range 0 to 65535. A single `char` can represent any character in the Basic Multilingual Plane, the first 65,536 Unicode code points. Characters beyond the BMP, called supplementary characters and including most emoji and many rare scripts, have code points above 65535 that do not fit in one 16-bit unit, so UTF-16 encodes them as a surrogate pair of two `char` values: a high surrogate in the range 0xD800 to 0xDBFF followed by a low surrogate in the range 0xDC00 to 0xDFFF. The `Character` helper methods `isHighSurrogate` and `isLowSurrogate` detect the halves, `Character.toCodePoint` combines a pair into the real code point, and `String.codePointAt` returns the full code point at an index, correctly handling surrogate pairs.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the bank's label printer can print any single symbol from a standard tray of 65,536 stamps, which covers almost every normal letter in every common language. But some special symbols, like a brand-new emoji on a payment note, are too big for one stamp, so the printer uses TWO stamps side by side that together mean one symbol, a high stamp and a low stamp. If Rajesh naively counts stamps, he thinks that one emoji is two characters and might cut a message in the middle of the pair, printing broken garbage. The Character and String helper methods are the trained operator who knows that a high stamp followed by a low stamp is really one symbol and handles them together.
s1_definition.oneliner: A char is one 16-bit UTF-16 code unit that covers the BMP; emoji and other supplementary characters need two chars, a surrogate pair, and you must use code-point methods to handle them correctly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Java `char` is a 16-bit unsigned integer type holding one UTF-16 code unit in the range 0 to 65535. A single `char` can represent any character in the Basic Multilingual Plane, the first 65,536 Unicode code points. Characters beyond the BMP, called supplementary characters and including most emoji and many rare scripts, have code points above 65535 that do not fit in one 16-bit unit, so UTF-16 encodes them as a surrogate pair of two `char` values: a high surrogate in the range 0xD800 to 0xDBFF followed by a low surrogate in the range 0xDC00 to 0xDFFF. The `Character` helper methods `isHighSurrogate` and `isLowSurrogate` detect the halves, `Character.toCodePoint` combines a pair into the real code point, and `String.codePointAt` returns the full code point at an index, correctly handling surrogate pairs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the bank's label printer can print any single symbol from a standard tray of 65,536 stamps, which covers almost every normal letter in every common language. But some special symbols, like a brand-new emoji on a payment note, are too big for one stamp, so the printer uses TWO stamps side by side that together mean one symbol, a high stamp and a low stamp. If Rajesh naively counts stamps, he thinks that one emoji is two characters and might cut a message in the middle of the pair, printing broken garbage. The Character and String helper methods are the trained operator who knows that a high stamp followed by a low stamp is really one symbol and handles them together.

**One line to remember:** A char is one 16-bit UTF-16 code unit that covers the BMP; emoji and other supplementary characters need two chars, a surrogate pair, and you must use code-point methods to handle them correctly.

sections.s2_technical:
A `char` is a 16-bit UNSIGNED value, which is unusual because every other Java integer type is signed. Its range is 0 to 65535, so `char c = 65;` is the letter A and `char max = '\uFFFF';` is the largest value. Because it is a numeric type under the hood, `char` participates in arithmetic: `'A' + 1` is 66 as an int, and you can cast back with `(char)('A' + 1)` to get B. Unicode escapes like `'\u20B9'` represent the rupee sign directly in source code.

The Basic Multilingual Plane is Unicode code points 0 through 65535, which includes Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, the main CJK characters, and most everyday symbols. Any BMP character fits in a single `char`. Supplementary characters live in planes above the BMP, with code points from 65536 up to 1,114,111. Examples include most emoji such as a rocket or a money-bag, mathematical alphanumeric symbols, and historic scripts. These do NOT fit in 16 bits.

UTF-16 represents a supplementary code point as a surrogate pair. The code point is split into two 16-bit halves: a high, or leading, surrogate in the reserved range 0xD800 to 0xDBFF, and a low, or trailing, surrogate in 0xDC00 to 0xDFFF. These ranges are reserved precisely so a decoder can tell a surrogate from a normal character. A Java `String` stores text as a sequence of UTF-16 code units, so a string containing one emoji has `length()` equal to 2, because length counts code units, not visual characters.

The helper methods let you work at the code-point level. `Character.isHighSurrogate(ch)` returns true if the char is a high surrogate, and `Character.isLowSurrogate(ch)` for a low surrogate, so you can detect that you are standing on the first half of a pair. `Character.toCodePoint(high, low)` combines the two halves into the full integer code point, for example turning a rocket's two surrogates into its code point 128640. On a String, `str.codePointAt(index)` returns the full code point beginning at that index, consuming both halves of a surrogate pair automatically, and `str.codePointCount(begin, end)` counts actual characters rather than code units. The idiomatic way to iterate real characters is `str.codePoints().forEach(cp -> ...)`, which yields code points directly.

Why this matters in practice: naive code that iterates `for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) s.charAt(i)` will visit each surrogate half separately, so it miscounts characters, can split a string in the middle of a pair, and can reverse text incorrectly, turning a valid emoji into two broken replacement characters. Database column sizing is affected too, because a varchar length in characters versus code units can differ. A senior engineer mentions that `substring` using code-unit indices can cut a surrogate pair, that uppercasing or lowercasing must be done on code points with a locale, and that when you truncate a customer note for an SMS you must truncate on code-point boundaries so you never emit half an emoji. The fix is to prefer code-point-aware APIs whenever input can contain supplementary characters, which today is routine because customers put emoji in payment notes.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India lets customers attach a short note to a payment, and those notes increasingly contain emoji, for example a gift payment with a money-bag or a celebration emoji. A real defect appeared when the note was processed character by character.

Problem 1 — the system counted a note's length with the plain length method and a character-by-character loop, so a note containing one emoji was counted as two characters, which threw off a length limit and a display truncation. This is exactly the difference between UTF-16 code units and real code points.

Problem 2 — the truncation logic cut a note to a fixed number of code units for an SMS gateway, and it occasionally cut right between a high surrogate and a low surrogate, emitting half of an emoji that rendered as a broken replacement box. This is exactly the surrogate-pair splitting hazard.

The fix uses code-point-aware methods. The length check counts code points with codePointCount, the truncation walks code points so it never splits a pair, and a small inspector shows how a single emoji decomposes into a high and low surrogate and how toCodePoint recombines them. The money amount itself is a BigDecimal and is never affected, but the note handling must be correct for display, storage sizing, and the SMS gateway.

The code defines an `Account`, a `PaymentNoteService` with a `charCount` method using codePointCount, a `safeTruncate` method that truncates on code-point boundaries, and an `inspectSurrogates` method using isHighSurrogate, isLowSurrogate, and toCodePoint. The demo processes a note containing an emoji for a transfer from Rajesh to Priya.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the money-bag emoji whose code point is hexadecimal 1F4B0, embedded in the note "Gift [emoji] for Priya".

Step 1. The emoji is built with Character.toChars of the code point 0x1F4B0, which returns a two-element char array because the code point is supplementary. As a String it is one visible character but two UTF-16 code units.

Step 2. The naive length call on the whole note returns the count of code units, so the single emoji contributes two to that count, making the note appear longer than it visually is. The service's charCount uses codePointCount, which counts the emoji as one real character, giving the correct visible length.

Step 3. The surrogate inspection reads charAt(0) and charAt(1) of the emoji. The first is a high surrogate in the 0xD800 to 0xDBFF range and the second is a low surrogate in the 0xDC00 to 0xDFFF range, which isHighSurrogate and isLowSurrogate confirm. Character.toCodePoint combines them back into 0x1F4B0, and codePointAt at index 0 returns the same value, proving both approaches agree.

Step 4. The safe truncation to seven code points measures the note in code points and walks exactly seven real characters using offsetByCodePoints, which returns a string index that lands on a safe boundary. Because the walk counts the emoji as one unit, the cut never lands between the two surrogate halves, so the output is "Gift [emoji]" with no broken replacement box.

Step 5. The demo logs the code-unit length, the real character count, the surrogate details, and the safely truncated note, then records that the note is stored for the transfer from Rajesh to Priya. The money amount is a BigDecimal elsewhere and is untouched by note handling.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 18:37:15 [WARNING] note.length() code units = 16
2026-10-30 18:37:15 [INFO] real character count = 15
2026-10-30 18:37:15 [INFO] recombined code point = U+1F4B0 (via codePointAt = U+1F4B0)
2026-10-30 18:37:15 [INFO] safe truncate to 7 chars = 'Gift 💰'
2026-10-30 18:37:15 [INFO] Transfer note stored for SAV2001 -> CUR3001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input note: "Gift 💰 for Priya"   (💰 = U+1F4B0, supplementary)
    │
    ▼
  String storage (UTF-16 code units)
    'G''i''f''t'' '  [D83D][DCB0]  ' ''f''o''r'...
                      ▲ high  ▲ low  = ONE emoji, TWO code units
    │
    ├─ note.length()        → 16  (code units — WRONG for display)
    ├─ codePointCount()     → 15  (real characters — correct)
    │
    ├─ inspectSurrogates(💰)
    │     charAt(0)=D83D → isHighSurrogate = true
    │     charAt(1)=DCB0 → isLowSurrogate  = true
    │     toCodePoint(D83D,DCB0) → U+1F4B0 ✓ (== codePointAt(0))
    │
    └─ safeTruncate(note, 7)
          offsetByCodePoints(0,7) → index AFTER the full emoji
          substring(0, idx) → "Gift 💰"  (never splits the pair)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — char, UTF-16 & Code Points ═══

  ┌─ Design Decisions ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Code-point-aware APIs everywhere a note may contain emoji:     │
  │     codePointCount, offsetByCodePoints, codePointAt, codePoints.│
  │  Never truncate by char index — may split a surrogate pair.     │

  ── Memory layout of a char / surrogate pair ────────────────────

  char  = 16-bit UNSIGNED  (range 0..65535)  → one BMP code unit
  BMP code point (0..65535)         → fits in ONE char
  Supplementary (65536..1114111)    → TWO chars (surrogate pair)
      high surrogate  D800..DBFF   +   low surrogate  DC00..DFFF

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │      PaymentNoteService      │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │
  │  + charCount(String): int    │  codePointCount
  │  + safeTruncate(String,int)  │  : String (offsetByCodePoints)
  │  + inspectSurrogates(String) │  isHigh/isLowSurrogate, toCodePoint
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │ annotates
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │           Account            │
  │  - balance: BigDecimal       │  ← money untouched by note logic
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. charCount(note) → codePointCount(0, length) → 15
  2. inspectSurrogates(💰): charAt(0)/charAt(1) → isHigh/isLow → toCodePoint
  3. safeTruncate(note, 7) → offsetByCodePoints(0,7) → substring(0, idx)

  Contract for safeTruncate(s, max):
    Pre:  max >= 0
    Post: returns a prefix of at most `max` CODE POINTS; never splits a pair
    Trap: substring(0, max) by char index can emit half a surrogate pair
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Java char is a sixteen-bit unsigned integer that holds one UTF-16 code unit, with a range from zero to sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-five. A single char can represent any character in the Basic Multilingual Plane, which is the first sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-six Unicode code points and covers the everyday characters of almost every common language. Because char is numeric under the hood and unsigned, it participates in arithmetic, so the letter A plus one is sixty-six as an int.

Characters beyond the BMP, called supplementary characters, have code points above sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-five, and these include most emoji and many rare scripts. They do not fit in a single sixteen-bit unit, so UTF-16 encodes them as a surrogate pair: a high surrogate in a reserved range followed by a low surrogate in another reserved range. A Java String stores text as UTF-16 code units, so a string containing one emoji has a length of two, because length counts code units rather than visible characters.

To handle supplementary characters correctly I use the code-point-aware methods. Character.isHighSurrogate and isLowSurrogate detect the two halves of a pair, Character.toCodePoint combines a high and low surrogate into the real code point, and on a String, codePointAt returns the full code point at an index while codePointCount counts real characters and offsetByCodePoints gives a safe boundary index. The failure mode I always warn about is naive code that loops over chars with charAt, because it visits each surrogate half separately, miscounts length, and can cut a string in the middle of a pair, emitting a broken replacement box.

In our payment-note feature at National Bank of India, customers started putting emoji in notes, and the original code counted length with the plain length method and truncated by char index for the SMS gateway. That counted one emoji as two characters and sometimes cut right between the two surrogates, sending half an emoji that rendered as a broken box. I fixed it by measuring length with codePointCount and truncating with offsetByCodePoints so the cut always lands on a code-point boundary and never splits a pair, and I made sure the database column used full Unicode storage. The money amount itself stayed a BigDecimal and was never touched by note handling, but getting the text handling right mattered for display, storage sizing, and the downstream SMS gateway.
